analysis.one_liner: Bars banks and financial institutions from discriminating by race, religion, national origin, or sex.
analysis.headline: A bill barring banks from discriminating against customers based on race, religion, national origin, or sex won 19 Senate sponsors and two committee hearings but died without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for financial institutions to refuse or limit services to someone because of race, color, religion, national origin, or sex — including sexual orientation and gender identity. Someone facing discrimination could go to federal court to stop it, and courts could award attorney's fees to the winner. It never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers — disproportionately Black, Latino, Muslim, Jewish, and LGBTQ people, who report being turned away or dropped by banks — would gain a federal right to full and equal access to banking services and a way to fight back in court.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits financial institutions from discriminating on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, or sex, explicitly including sexual orientation and gender identity.
Gives an aggrieved person a private right of action to seek preventive relief — an injunction or restraining order — in federal court, without first exhausting administrative remedies.
Lets courts award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party, so a person who cannot afford a lawyer can still sue.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other financial institutions would bear the cost: they could no longer decline or restrict service on prohibited grounds and would face the risk of federal lawsuits, plus attorney's fees if they lose.

drawbacks.text: The remedy is limited: the bill provides only preventive relief such as injunctions, so a customer who was denied service could stop future discrimination but could not recover money damages under this section.

Banks would face new litigation exposure, and some institutions argue they exit customers or industries — such as certain cash-intensive or high-risk businesses — for legal-risk reasons rather than prejudice; a broad prohibition could complicate those decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would establish a clear federal right to equal access to banking, which matters most to people from groups that report being 'debanked' or refused service. The main cost falls on financial institutions in the form of litigation risk and compliance. The design has a real limit — no money damages, only court orders to stop discrimination — which makes enforcement harder for individuals but also keeps the exposure for banks lower than a full damages regime.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held two hearings, but it was never brought to the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on July 26, 2022, with 18 Senate cosponsors — 17 Democrats and 1 independent — and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The Banking Committee held hearings on September 22, 2022, and December 1, 2022, but the bill never advanced to a markup or a Senate floor vote.
No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without a vote on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and financial institutions are better off because the bill died: they face no new federal nondiscrimination obligation or private lawsuits over who they serve. People who report being refused or dropped by banks got no new remedy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks, which face no new rules

for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OH); bill sponsor and Chair, Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 18 Senate cosponsors; as Banking chair, held hearings on it.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent — 17 of 48 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 2 independents — and no Republican senator signed on.

industries.note: The bill would strip banks of the ability to decline or restrict service on the basis of race, religion, national origin, or sex, and expose them to federal injunction suits and attorney's fees. Banks' interest in avoiding these obligations runs directly against customers' interest in equal access to banking.
